items.source: second reader345 and own original-source review
items.finding: interpretation_gap.claimed
items.reason: The abstract concludes that "Telescoping is a relatively robust phenomenon in treatment-seeking alcoholics" and that women are more likely to progress faster through the landmarks (p. 252); the Discussion speaks of strong support (p. 257), recommends identifying women at the loss-of-control stage for intensive intervention and alerting women that they are more likely than men to develop alcohol problems and dependence rapidly (p. 259), and offers biological explanations (higher blood alcohol from body size and composition, gastric first-pass metabolism, organ toxicity, hormones) and social or psychiatric ones, none of which was measured (p. 258). Gaps: (1) a recruitment-age explanation is plausible but conditional: Table1 similar entry ages refer to all1589, while the treatment interval concerns735 with no sex-specific entry ages. The comparisons below use different samples and do not decompose the observed treatment difference: in the editors' reading of Figure 1, the men–women gaps in time to treatment by quintile (about 0.8, 2.0, 4.5, 7.7 and 6.5 years) are close to the gaps in age at getting drunk regularly in Table 2 (0.8, 1.8, 4.1, 7.1 and 7.1); the interval ending at the worst period, reached at the same age by both sexes, is affected in the same way; (2) the effects are small (ω² .01 to .04), which the authors acknowledge (pp. 255, 259), and absent in the youngest quintile, so 'relatively robust' overstates them; (3) alerting women in general extends a treatment-sample finding to all women; (4) the landmark ages were recalled, and only 53% of participants reported the assumed order. The limitations paragraph names the exclusion of people dependent on other drugs (p. 259) but not the selection at treatment entry.

items.finding:
No causal overstatement. Wording points: (1) the opening sentence counts the twins' outcome among 'lifetime drug use disorders', but for drugs this study's abuse/dependence is a simplified symptom count (abuse = either of 2 abuse symptoms; dependence = 2 or more of 4 dependence symptoms), asked only of people who used a drug at least monthly, which the authors say does not provide formal DSM-IV criteria (p. 429); only alcohol dependence used full DSM-IV criteria. 'Drug abuse or dependence as the study defined it' would be exact. (2) 'the twin who started early more often reported any illicit drug abuse or dependence': 'met the study's criteria for' is more exact than 'reported'. (3) 'no separate estimates for identical pairs' is right for what is printed; the paper says separate identical- and fraternal-pair analyses (with cut-offs of 15, 16 and 18) confirmed its conclusions but shows no numbers (p. 431), so 'none reported' would be exact. (4) 'factors that differ between co-twins, such as friends, were measured only in part' can be read as friends being partly measured; friends or peers were not measured at all (the within-pair covariates were early tobacco and alcohol use, conduct disorder, major depression and social anxiety).
All Lynskey numbers in the statement and magnitude match the rendered pages (Figure and Methods p. 428; Table 2 p. 430). Recomputed: 2765/4010 = 69%; 74 + 62 = 136 identical and 84 + 91 = 175 fraternal pairs; 234 + 77 = 311; every Table 2 percentage = n/311. 'Lowered the odds ratios by up to about a fifth': largest fall 19.4% (sedative use 2.83 to 2.28); any drug abuse/dependence 11.6%, alcohol dependence 14.7%, cannabis abuse/dependence 8.0%, several unchanged; correct. '311 of the 407 discordant pairs': the concordance analysis (p. 430) counts 88 + 110 + 98 + 111 = 407 discordant same-sex pairs against 311 analysed (62 of 88 identical male, 74 of 98 identical female, 91 of 110 fraternal male, 84 of 111 fraternal female), with no explanation: confirmed. In addition, its 229 concordant pairs imply 2 x 229 + 407 = 865 early starters among complete same-sex pairs, more than the 861 early starters reported for all 6,265 people interviewed (p. 428 and Figure), so the concordance counts and the sample-flow figure cannot both be right. Other reporting points: the adjusted alcohol-dependence OR 1.85 (1.21-2.83) is printed identically in Table 2 (311 pairs; unadjusted 2.17) and Table 3 (234 pairs; unadjusted 2.03), so one is probably a copying error, and the claim's adjusted figure rests on Table 2; the Comment's ranges of 2.3- to 3.9-fold and 1.6- to 6.0-fold (p. 431) are those of Table 3 (234 pairs), not of the main analysis summarised in the abstract (2.1 to 5.2); the 17 people who began another drug before cannabis are said to have been excluded from the analyses (p. 430), yet every Table 2 percentage still uses 311; the 24.8% of twins said to report no lifetime cannabis use (p. 430) is 77 of 311 co-twins, i.e. 12.4% of the 622 twins. Where both twins had used cannabis (234 pairs) cannabis abuse/dependence was only marginal after adjustment (1.57, 0.98-2.52, P = .06; Table 3, p. 431).
